items.title: The Decade’s 10 Most Defining Movies (So Far)
items.description: This is an edition of Video Village , David Sims’s newsletter that unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession. Sign up for it here. Welcome to Video Village, a new space for The Atlantic ’s film-loving readers. For this, my first edition, my editors challenged me to lay out my perspective on my own taste, so I’ve worked up a list of movies that I think define this strange decade thus far. These are all personal favorites, yes, but this is not precisely a “best of” list; think more an atmospheric overview of how Hollywood looks and operates today, which will be a recurring theme of this newsletter. Let’s get two of the most obvious picks out of the way: Greta Gerwig’s Barbie and Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer , whose release on the same day in July 2023—and during a strike that kneecapped Hollywood —resulted in a multibillion-dollar cultural phenomenon. The industry has spent the following years trying its darndest to recapture that success—and to undo the coronavirus pandemic’s unprecedented effects on moviegoing as a whole. Those movies aside, here’s a look at 10 other great films that illustrate the spirit of the 2020s. Da 5 Bloods (2020, directed by Spike Lee): The decade kicked off with what still has been its oddest year, defined by COVID lockdowns, theaters going out of business, and the dominance of streaming services at a moment when the only way to experience good movies (for most people) was at home. A lot of the wonderful films released that year feel like a blur; maybe the best example of a memory-holed masterpiece is Lee’s Vietnam epic, Da 5 Bloods , which I’d love to someday see on a giant screen with booming sound. It boldly ties the failures of America’s intervention in that war to the country’s struggles since, with Delroy Lindo’s troubled vet turned MAGA patriot the chief emblem of its chaotic viewpoint. Hopefully, this ambitious movie, whose production was similarly fascinating , will be rediscovered in the years ahead—ideally on a bigger screen than a television set. The Worst Person in the World (2021, directed by Joachim Trier): The ultimate work of self-reflexive Millennial-core, the Norwegian director Trier’s sharp dramedy came just as some moviegoers were returning to theaters after lockdowns had frozen them in time and anxiety. It follows Julie (played by Renate Reinsve), a witty 30-year-old who simply does not know what to do with her life. The film charts her every stutter-step career decision and corresponding romantic entanglements with bittersweet aplomb. All of Trier’s movies are worth checking out (the most recent being Sentimental Value , a hit at this year’s Oscars). But this one remains my personal favorite. Drive My Car (2021, directed by Ryusuke Hamaguchi): One of the best examples of William Goldman’s notorious industry adage—“Nobody knows anything”—is this three-hour, soft-spoken Japanese drama. The story of a depressed theater director’s effort to stage a multilingual production of Uncle Vanya became a surprise sensation, launching Hamaguchi to art-house fame and snagging four major Oscar nominations, including Best Picture. It’s a beautiful work of deceptive tranquility, where aloof conversations belie dark emotional storms beneath; it’s also the greatest adaptation of Haruki Murakami’s writing ever put to film. Hamaguchi has since proved to be one of the decade’s most fascinating auteurs, and his work is appointment viewing. (Next up is All of a Sudden , out this November.) Tár (2022, directed by Todd Field): I finally became convinced that the theater experience wasn’t going anywhere while watching the titular protagonist of Tár , Lydia (Cate Blanchett), confront a child who had bullied her daughter on the playground—I felt the entire viewing audience ripple with delight. Here we all were, observing this egotistical conductor whose life was spiraling to pieces, and struggling to resist the urge to cheer for such obviously aberrant behavior. Field’s film is a fantastic portrayal of ego, power, and the kind of rapid professional disintegration that’s become more common in the celebrity sphere of late; it’s a totally unique take on a common spectacle. Nope (2022, directed by Jordan Peele): Peele announced himself as a film director with the subversive smash that was Get Out and could have led his career in any direction from there. I love that he’s instead doubled down on original horror storytelling. Nope is his most recent movie (a new project is supposedly in the works but remains a mystery), and it’s his best and most ambitious: a sly tale of how the entertainment world can chew people up and spit them out. It also features a flying monster that can literally do that. RRR (2022, directed by S. S. Rajamouli): This epic from India’s Telugu-language industry (known as “Tollywood”) blasted into multiplexes out of nowhere, just as the Hollywood blockbuster began truly spooling up again. RRR showed Americans how grandiose, CGI-assisted action filmmaking can still feel fun and original; the movie is a sprawling, 1920s-set musical epic of revolt and revenge designed to inspire viewers to stand and applaud throughout. The crowd-pleaser par excellence broke records around the world and even won an Oscar for Best Original Song. Rajamouli’s much-anticipated next film, Varanasi , is due for release in 2027. Asteroid City (2023, directed by Wes Anderson): Few raves I’ve written in my time at The Atlantic have been more polarizing than my championing of Anderson’s sci-fi comedy; multiple people who had grown wary of the writer-director’s output have angrily confronted me about my review. Plenty of readers, however, agree with me wholeheartedly that it’s the director’s best film in close to a decade. Whatever other viewers make of it (and all of Anderson’s recent work, which is hermetic and tightly designed even by his standards), I think Asteroid City is one of the most profound attempts to wrestle with the odd sense of community and tragedy that emerged when most of us were unable to leave our home. It’s a very modern portrait of quarantine—albeit set in the 1950s—that doesn’t pull its punches on the darkness that its broad ensemble is struggling with. Red Rooms (2024, directed by Pascal Plante): Looking back at 2020s cinema, we’ll find that a defining trend was contending with the spiraling madness of online life. Red Rooms is maybe the best horror movie ever made about being on your computer too much: The Canadian thriller is a freaky tale of a true crime–obsessed woman (Juliette Gariépy) fixated on a murder case that’s sparked a media circus. It’s a profoundly disturbing watch, even though it holds back on graphic visuals (like many a great horror movie, it leaves the worst to your imagination). Red Rooms was a sneaky festival hit before it trickled into cinemas, and it’s guaranteed to become a long-running cult classic. Eddington (2025, directed by Ari Aster) : This internet-horror story runs right at the bizarre experience of the pandemic lockdowns. Aster’s Eddington was profoundly divisive on release and was quickly dismissed by some critics for its sheer unpleasantness. It’s worth a watch (or, if you hated it the first time, a revisit); Aster’s got a keen eye for the type of online brain poisoning that has grown and spread across the world over the past six years, and he has a darkly humorous perspective on the way identity politics have been misappropriated by bad actors. I had barely heard of data centers when I saw Eddington last summer; now they are often at the top of political discourse. What else did Aster see coming? Backrooms (2026, directed by Kane Parsons): I’m hardly proclaiming Backrooms the movie of the year; 2026 isn’t even over yet. But its release definitely seems to have pushed Hollywood to recognize a new frontier in filmmaking. The horror film, a bewildering adaptation of a series of YouTube videos, was directed by a 20-year-old who taught himself visual-effects technology during high school. Set in a world of eerie liminal spaces, Backrooms feels somehow beamed in from another universe while also being a slick creep-fest that could draw in young viewers on “vibes” alone. The unsettling promise of its scares just feels so unlike anything I’ve seen in theaters lately—I loved it. An Essay I Enjoyed Robert Falconer / Prime Carrie , With Kid Gloves By Emma Stefansky The climax of Carrie , Stephen King’s debut horror novel, is so famous that even people who haven’t read it or seen any of the numerous adaptations know the basics. The eponymous Carrie White, driven to the edge of sanity after years of abuse from her classmates and hyper-religious mother, gets drenched in a bucket of pig’s blood at her prom. She then uses her latent telekinetic powers to destroy her high school and her hometown. It’s an extreme reaction to an extreme situation, the climax of a revenge story in which vengeance is just another tragic act of violence. The line between villain and victim blurs. Read the full article. Coming Attractions October tends to mark the start of a real glut of releases: Many major premieres happen in quick succession at big fall festivals (in Telluride, Venice, Toronto, and New York), and then they come to regular theatergoers—and bring the awards race into focus. One of this year’s contenders, in theaters this week, is Fjord . Directed by the Romanian auteur Cristian Mungiu, it won him the Palme d’Or at this summer’s Cannes Film Festival—an award that has become a bit of a springboard to more mainstream success, as it did for the recent Best Picture winners Anora and Parasite . But I’m of two minds on whether Fjord will follow in their footsteps. Like all of Mungiu’s movies, it is challenging in its remoteness, asking the audience to hold some uncomfortable truths and make their own decisions about them. The film follows a Romanian family that has immigrated to a remote Norwegian village. The parents, played by Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, are both stern and religious, placing them well outside of the country’s secular cultural norms. The couple is soon accused of abuse, and the government takes their children away while an investigation proceeds—a situation that erupts into something of an international incident. The reality of what’s happening is plain to grasp: This parenting style is at best alienating, and the seemingly tolerant society surrounding the family doesn’t quite know how to deal with it. Fjord is grim, and at 146 minutes, it’s a demanding watch—one that may be too disaffecting to break through. But it’s also an undeniably engrossing experience; no character feels truly sympathetic, and best intentions crumble in the face of internet outrage and ill-functioning bureaucracy. What Else I’m Watching I rewatched Paweł Pawlikowski’s film Cold War in preparation for the upcoming release of Fatherland , which will complete a loose trilogy about postwar Europe; it’s short, sometimes sexy, and sweetly tragic (and streaming on Prime Video). I’m also catching up on the filmography of another great director, Lee Chang-dong, whose Possible Love is out at the end of the month (and in November on Netflix). I watched his debut, Green Fish , which is a lovely and poetic little crime saga from 1997. (It’s available to rent on Prime Video and Apple TV, and streaming on Kanopy, though I watched it on a disc published by Vinegar Syndrome.) Finally, I caught up with last year’s documentary Pompei: Below the Clouds , from Gianfranco Rosi. It’s a gorgeous and fragmented portrayal of life in modern Naples in the shadow of Mount Vesuvius, and it’s streaming on Mubi.

items.title: Confessions of a Bad Texter
items.description: Illustrations by Hannah Robinson Whenever I receive a text , this is what happens. I pick up my phone. So far, so good. I experience whatever emotion the message elicits—the pleasant warmth of being reached out to, possibly the annoyance of being interrupted. Then, if conditions are right, if I’m not too busy or in the middle of talking with someone else, if my mind is at peace, if my anxiety is at no more than a low hum, if Mercury is not in retrograde, I will respond right then and there. If conditions are not right, it will be as though the text never existed at all. Right now, I have 30 unopened texts. Scrolling through my messages, I find several more that I opened but forgot to respond to for anywhere between a few hours and a week and a half—from my parents, my sister’s fiancé, old friends who are accustomed to this kind of behavior, and new friends who are just beginning to be disappointed in me. At least two people texted me so long ago—more than a month—that to respond now and remind them how long they’ve been waiting would be worse than not responding at all. I’m not proud of leaving people hanging. Every text I owe is a tiny siren in the back of my mind, blaring intermittent pulses of guilt. Unless I forget about it entirely, in which case I’ll remember it with a shameful jolt some days or weeks later. I’m not one of those modern hermits who thinks you don’t owe anyone anything, who likes every Instagram post she sees about boundaries and thinks that flaking on plans is self-care. I write about relationships for a living, and I believe that showing up for one another is the purpose of our existence. That’s, like, my whole brand. And so this is my greatest shame: I am a Bad Texter. I am slow to respond. I am forgetful. I get overwhelmed. My own mother has said I’m “probably worse than 90 percent of the other people that I text with.” This might seem like a trivial pathology, but it isn’t. Texting is the currency of modern relationships. In 2024, Americans exchanged more than 2 trillion text messages, about 42 billion more than the year before, according to CTIA , a trade group representing the wireless industry. Some of those texts are probably spam. Some are advertising. Some are bits of automated busywork ( click this link to confirm your appointment ). But many of them, hopefully most of them, are between people who know one another, reaching out for connection over the waves of the wireless spectrum. According to a 2023 survey , texting is the No. 1 way that people prefer to communicate with their loved ones, beating out mobile-phone calls and absolutely crushing face-to-face conversations, which got only 8 percent of the vote. Texting came out ahead in every age bracket except the oldest; those 55 and older ranked texting and mobile-phone calls equally. No age group preferred anything over texting. Yet at the same time, texting stresses people out. A third of Americans report feeling overwhelmed by the number of texts they need to respond to, and a majority say they struggle to keep up with their group chats. As Pranav Malhotra, who studies communication and media at the University of Michigan, told me, texting “is what the people want, but it’s not doing them any good.” And so, many of us end up feeling like Bad Texters. We are here, we are legion, and we are sorry for our delayed response. Texting dominates our social lives like nothing else. According to the research firm Nielsen, American cellphone users started texting more than they called in 2007 . Since then, unlimited phone plans and widespread Wi-Fi have removed many of the barriers that once led people to restrict their texts. The ubiquity of text-messaging hardly seems worth questioning—it’s simply the way things are. But when you think about it, the modern predilection for managing all of our relationships by typing on a tiny touch screen is a bit odd. “For darn sure, it’s a lot faster to talk about things than it is to text them,” Naomi Baron, who studies language and technology at American University, told me. “Particularly if you have more than, let’s say, 100 characters’ worth to say. But it’s become the way of doing things.” Texting achieved domination because it’s convenient—you can message someone at any time without waiting to see if they’re available first—and because it offers a sense of control. You don’t need to risk the uncertainty that comes with live conversation; you can plan out exactly what you want to say, and people won’t see how you react to their response. This is one of the things that people say they like best about texting. But the ease of sending messages means, on the flip side, that people are receiving more. [ Listen: Would you go back to a time before smartphones if you could? ] As texting became our default mode of communication, messages that once might have taken another form—your hair salon calling to confirm an appointment, an email invite to your best friend’s birthday party, a paper medical bill—started arriving as texts. And the act of texting is no longer confined to whatever mobile app processes your SMS messages. I have four different texting-specific apps on my phone: the standard iPhone Messages, WhatsApp, Signal, and KakaoTalk—a Korean messaging app where my in-laws’ family group chat lives. Then there are social-media DMs, which function much like texting, and Slack, where my colleagues send me DMs that would have been emails not so long ago. These show up on my home screen as notifications, and when I respond on my phone, the feeling is very similar to texting. I have sometimes attempted to deal with my texting overwhelm by communicating in other ways. Lately, I’ve been trying to call people more to catch up, which is wonderful, but it can also cause alarm. One British survey from 2024 found that more than half of young adults said they assumed unexpected calls meant bad news. (Surely you would just text anything else you want to say.) Sometimes I’ll send my friends voice messages when I want to tell them a story that’s too long to type, but this, too, is controversial. I love voice messages—I think they feel so much more intimate than a text—but many people think that expecting a friend to take five minutes out of their day to listen to a mini-podcast you recorded is annoying, or even selfish. For party invitations, vacation planning, or anything logistical, I prefer to use email, but I’ve received explicit feedback from my husband and many of my friends that I should be texting instead, because “no one checks their email.” (Can this possibly be true?) Whenever I try to escape, social pressure always seems to push me back to texting. And so the texts multiply, taking up more and more space in our relationships, until to be called a Bad Texter feels like being accused of being a bad spouse, sibling, child, parent, or friend. Hannah Robinson Instagram’s algorithm must have me figured out because it recently served me a video of an episode of “SubwayTakes,” in which the comedian Delaney Rowe shared her take : “There’s no such thing as a bad texter; they just don’t want to respond.” Claiming to be bad at texting, she said, is a “cop-out,” because a lack of responsiveness is conditional. “When a bad texter gets a crush? Best texter in the world,” she said. This is what I fear my loved ones think: that my response time is directly correlated with how much I care about them. What else could it be? Americans check their phone nearly 200 times a day on average, and the overwhelming majority keep their phone on them “almost all the time,” according to recent surveys. The modern expectation that everyone is constantly reachable is unreasonable, but it’s not that unreasonable, given how attached people are to their phones. Lizzie Post is a great-great-granddaughter of the early-20th-century etiquette writer Emily Post, and a co-president of the Emily Post Institute, where she writes about modern manners. Unfortunately, she confirmed that politeness requires responding to texts promptly, and that too long a delay is rude. (Though the meaning of promptly can vary depending on the context.) “I hate to say it,” she told me, but “I would really try to prioritize it a bit more.” She was not the only expert I spoke with who said I needed to shape up. “Get one with the idea that people who text expect fast responses,” Paul Leonardi, a technology-management professor at UC Santa Barbara and the author of Digital Exhaustion , told me. You don’t have to meet that expectation, but there are consequences for not doing so. He pointed out that, especially with long-distance loved ones, a text thread is “the meat of our relationship.” A shared experience is happening there, and you’re either contributing to it or you’re not. Often, he advised, it’s better to just say something—anything—quickly, rather than waiting to form the perfect response later. (I do sometimes delay texting people because I want to wait until I can put more thought into my message. But the longer I wait, the better I feel the message needs to be to justify the delay. The pressure builds.) Post agreed. By responding too slowly, I’m at risk, she said, of making people think I don’t want to connect with them—even if that’s not true. One of the costs of conducting so much of our relationships via text is the loss of context. In exchange for convenience, we give up tone of voice, eye contact, and body language. When all we have to go on are the words in front of us (or the lack thereof), we tend to “overinterpret very minor cues as signals of rudeness or as signals of Oh, this person doesn’t care about me ,” Gretchen McCulloch, a linguist who studies online communication and the author of Because Internet, told me. Hence the unwritten rule that putting a period at the end of a text is passive-aggressive. My mom recently had a serious dustup with a friend, seemingly just because my mom put the word not in all caps in a text. Gaps in information too often get filled in with projections and insecurities. I know my haphazard approach to texting risks fanning just such insecurities. And I’ve tried to be better. I put responding to texts on my to-do list. I’ve tried not opening any texts until I’m ready to write back, letting the notifications pile up and remind me every time I open my phone. I made a calendar reminder for every day at 4 p.m. that says “RESPOND TO TEXTS!!!,” following the advice of several experts who suggested setting aside time to deal with all my texts at once, rather than taking them as they come. This helps, although it also makes me feel like I’m treating my loved ones like a productivity problem instead of a source of joy. And there’s nothing to stop me from ignoring the reminder the same way I would a text. Social obligation is as old as human society. In the 19th century, the practice of making social “calls” seems to have produced a feeling similar to the anxiety I get when I open my texts. An 1895 column in the Rocky Mountain News declared that the problem was one of volume—there were simply too many calls that one was expected to pay. “It may certainly be a pleasure to visit one’s friends,” the anonymous author wrote, but the pleasure fades “when you are meeting them every day almost, by dozens and scores and hundreds.” One woman quoted seemed to be on the verge of a nervous breakdown: “The calls I owe haunt me. They rise up in my dreams and chase me with spectre fingers.” Falling behind on your correspondence is nothing new, either. “The guilty message—‘I’m sorry it took me so long to respond’—has a very long history,” Steven Mintz, a historian at the University of Texas at Austin, told me. Indeed, in the 1922 edition of Emily Post’s Etiquette , the author writes, “One of the frequent difficulties in beginning a letter is that your answer is so long delayed that you begin with an apology, which is always a lame duck.” The difference is that although an unanswered letter may have caused guilt and anxiety, you weren’t expected to respond to it within five minutes. Technology has taken our sense of social obligation, accelerated it, amplified it, and splintered it into billions of little green and blue bubbles, each one both a point of connection and a task hanging over our heads . “People always say we’re wired to connect, but this isn’t the kind of connecting that we’re wired for,” Lori Gottlieb, a psychotherapist and the author of Maybe You Should Talk to Someone , told me. Being a Bad Texter might harm your relationships, but being a Good Texter will not necessarily help them. Research is unclear on this front. In terms of connection, texting seems to be better than nothing, but nowhere near as beneficial as phone calls or face-to-face conversations. The latter are definitely good for us, and they’re declining. Time-use data show that over the past couple of decades, Americans have been spending less time socializing in person . One study even found that the number of words people speak out loud each day has decreased. [ From the February 2025 issue: Derek Thompson on the anti-social century ] Some research has suggested that the more someone texts, the lonelier and less satisfied they feel. In one study, researchers theorized that people found texting exasperating because they were using it with the intention of keeping in touch, but it didn’t actually do all that much to maintain relationships. And every text message is a little interruption, taxing your attention and taking focus from the people who may be right in front of you. Nothing in the research definitively says we shouldn’t be texting one another—but nothing says we should prioritize it the way we do, either. “The one thing that’s consistent about it is that it’s inconsistent,” Jess Dominguez, who researches communication at the University of Kentucky, told me. Technology, she said, “is always good and bad, and always at the same time.” The overwhelming emotion associated with texting seems to be ambivalence. The same things that make texting appealing also make it stressful. It’s easy; it’s convenient; it can be done anytime, anywhere. But that means you can end up feeling like you should be available to respond all the time, everywhere. Texting allows you to keep up with more people at once than phone calls or letters ever did. But those exchanges are shallower and less fulfilling. It gives welcome control over communication, but that can lead to pressure to draft the ideal response, or to using texting as a shield to hide from the messiness of real-time conversation. It is fun and it is frustrating, and it doesn’t really matter if you like it, because it is more powerful than you are, and it’s not going anywhere. Hannah Robinson Eventually, we all must do things we have been dreading, whether it is apologizing for not texting someone back for a month or, in my case, interviewing my friends and family for this article. A story like this requires a reckoning, and narratively, I recognized that I must face up to who I am and what I have done to those I love. But I didn’t want to, and I put it off as long as I could, until just before my deadline. Feedback was kind, but mixed. “I have no complaints,” my husband said. Vindication?! But “my bar is very low.” Oh. A friend of mine called my failure to respond to a dinner invite until the day of “chaotic.” When I asked my parents how their experience texting with me has been, my dad immediately said, “Poor.” He had recently sent me a Mountain Goats song he likes; I hadn’t responded. “A little too much to ask that you put a heart?” he said, only half-joking. “Couldn’t do it, could you?” My mom said she’s never been offended, only confused. “I always walk this line between: Did she see the text, couldn’t answer it, and then forgot about it? Or did she see the text and she’s still going to answer it? It’s, like, this waiting thing,” she said. “Should I remind her? Should I not remind her?” Several people told me they didn’t think of me as a notably Bad Texter, or at least they weren’t bothered by my slowness. My friend Morgan pointed out that a text, like any other form of communication, is a “bid for connection.” But it’s different than if someone opened their arms for a hug and I just walked away. Although I may drop the ball on responding sometimes, Morgan said, “I don’t feel like you’ve ever dropped the ball on maintaining a connection.” I once read somewhere that trying to keep up with your work emails is a trap. The emails will never stop coming, and your only reward for responding quickly will be more emails. So you have two choices: You can be good at responding to email or you can be good at your job. [ Listen: What it takes to reclaim your attention span ] I feel a similar way about keeping up with my texts. I suppose I could opt out entirely and throw my phone into the sea. But opting out of texting would mean, to some degree, choosing isolation. I don’t want people to stop reaching out to me; I don’t want to give up on the good parts of texting, even if they’re inextricable from the bad. So I will try to carve out the occasional hour to attend to my correspondence. But I also want to let go of some of the guilt that tells me every delayed response means I’m being a bad friend, daughter, sister, wife. I bring other things to the table, after all. If you need practical help—someone to feed your pets, watch your kids, help you move—I would be delighted to provide it. I’ll make spreadsheets to plan our vacations. I’ll buy you little gifts, and alarm you with cold calls just to catch up. If we’re together, I’ll put my phone away and give you my full attention . But if you text me, you may not hear back for a while. You can be good at texting. You can be good at your relationships. Maybe for some people, it’s possible to be both. But they are not the same thing. We want to hear from you: Tell us how many unread messages you have—or send a screenshot!—along with your name and the reason you’re not-so-great at responding promptly. Text your response to (202) 266-7715 . (By participating, you agree to grant The Atlantic permission to use, modify, and distribute your submission text in all media.) This article appears in the November 2026 print edition with the headline “Confessions of a Bad Texter.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

items.title: Artificial stability or sustainable equilibrium? Rethinking the Cedi’s performance
items.description: My assessments of Ghana’s fiscal dynamics and monetary developments have consistently been grounded in the underlying economic fundamentals. When the government initially attributed the cedi’s improved performance primarily to fiscal consolidation, I challenged that interpretation and argued that substantial interventions by the Bank of Ghana (BoG) in the foreign-exchange market were a major, if not the principal, factor underpinning the observed stability. At the time, this position attracted considerable criticism. Subsequently, however, assessments by the World Bank and the IMF lent support to the argument that BoG interventions had played a significant role in sustaining the currency’s stability. The President eventually acknowledged the importance of such interventions, while the Governor of the BoG publicly identified foreign-exchange interventions as an important contributor to the cedi’s performance, a position that differed from some of his earlier public pronouncements. More recently, I have faced criticism from KSM and other NDC commentators for characterising the current stability of the cedi as partly artificial. Some senior CSO actors sympathetic to the NDC have also consistently ridiculed this position. However, the fundamental economic argument remains straightforward: exchange-rate stability that is heavily dependent on sustained central-bank intervention cannot, by itself, constitute a durable equilibrium. If the capacity or willingness of the central bank to intervene is constrained, the underlying pressures on the domestic currency are likely to re-emerge. My central argument has therefore been that a sustainable and resilient cedi requires attention to the structural foundations of the Ghanaian economy rather than excessive reliance on foreign-exchange interventions. Policy should focus particularly on expanding domestic production in agriculture and manufacturing, reducing excessive dependence on imports, and strengthening the country’s export capacity. A stronger productive base would have several important macroeconomic benefits. Increased domestic production would reduce the demand for foreign exchange associated with imports, while greater export capacity would increase foreign-exchange earnings. This would reduce the pressure on the BoG to continually inject foreign currency into the market to support the cedi. At the same time, expanding agriculture and manufacturing could generate employment, broaden the domestic tax base, and enhance the government’s capacity to mobilise resources internally. The recent developments in the foreign-exchange market provide an important test of this argument. Over the past two months, the cedi has increasingly shown signs of depreciation following the BoG’s decision to reduce its previous practice of supplying approximately US$1 billion monthly to the foreign-exchange market. Under the emerging arrangement, the GoldBod is expected to play a greater role in foreign-exchange intermediation. Commercial banks provide credit to GoldBod to finance gold purchases, after which GoldBod provides foreign currency to the banks following the sale of the gold. Conceptually, this arrangement may represent a more sustainable mechanism than continuous direct intervention by the central bank. Nevertheless, its effectiveness will depend significantly on the availability of gold and credit, as well as developments in international gold prices. This raises important questions about the resilience of the arrangement. What happens if the supply of gold declines substantially? What happens if efforts to curb illegal mining significantly reduce gold production? And what happens if international gold prices experience a prolonged decline? These are not merely theoretical questions. An exchange-rate strategy that relies heavily on a single commodity as the principal source of foreign-exchange liquidity exposes the economy to significant external and domestic risks. Ghana therefore needs to think beyond short-term currency stabilisation mechanisms. No serious long-term economic strategy should depend excessively on commodity-based foreign-exchange inflows to sustain currency stability. The more fundamental solution lies in transforming the productive structure of the economy: increasing agricultural and industrial output, reducing import dependence, diversifying exports, expanding domestic value addition, and strengthening the country’s capacity to generate foreign exchange through a broad range of productive activities. Ultimately, the objective should not simply be to defend the cedi. The objective should be to build an economy in which the cedi does not require perpetual defence.

items.title: GIPA CEO calls for investment to support Ghana’s economic transformation
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority (GIPA), Simon Madjie has called for increased investment, technology and expertise to help turn Ghana’s emerging economic opportunities into productive businesses and sustainable jobs. According to him, the Big Push Infrastructure Programme, 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme and the New Economy Programme are creating opportunities for investors to participate in infrastructure development, domestic production, industrialisation and export growth. Mr Madjie made the call at the launch of the Invest Ghana Summit 2026 and the 22nd Ghana Club 100 Awards, being organised by GIPA in collaboration with its partners. He said recent improvements in the economy, including stronger growth, declining inflation, rising international reserves and a more stable exchange rate, had provided a stronger foundation for investment. He added that the development of a productive economy required the mobilisation of capital, technology and expertise to support businesses, create jobs and expand exports. Mr. Madjie also highlighted the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173), saying the new law had removed general minimum foreign capital requirements for joint ventures and wholly foreign-owned enterprises. He further stated that the legislation had also strengthened investor protections and expanded GIPA’s mandate to provide more effective and coordinated support to investors. He opined that the investment environment was therefore being reformed alongside the implementation of programmes designed to expand economic activity.

items.title: Gaza, 3 ans après : "le génocide est toujours en cours" pour le journaliste Rami Abou Jamus
items.description: Trois ans après les attaques du Hamas du 7-Octobre, les regards se tournent aujourd’hui vers Gaza. Un fragile cessez-le-feu est en place depuis un an, mais la bande de Gaza reste largement dévastée et la population fait face à des conditions de vie extrêmement difficiles, notamment pour se nourrir et accéder aux services essentiels. Nous évoquons la vie quotidienne à Gaza avec Rami Abou Jamus, journaliste indépendant sur place, qui parle de « Gazastrophe » et estime que « le génocide est toujours en cours », malgré une baisse du niveau des bombardements.

items.title: Basket : Amina Seck retrouve la liberté après deux mois de détention aux États-Unis
items.description: La basketteuse sénégalaise Amina Seck a été libérée après plusieurs semaines passées en détention aux États-Unis. Elle avait été interpellée le 7 août par des agents de l'ICE , l'agence américaine de l'immigration, à l'aéroport de Louisville, alors qu'elle se rendait avec son équipe à un tournoi à New York. Pour sa première prise de parole, la joueuse a suligné la rudesse de l’épreuve. « Je voudrais juste dire Alhamdoulilah, remercier Dieu pour tout ce qu’il a fait durant cette épreuve. Je voudrais remercier toutes les personnes qui m’ont aidée et prié pour moi. Ce fut difficile, mais comme on dit, tout ce qui arrive est bon. Je suis prête à retourner à l’université, à obtenir mon master et à me faire opérer », confie la jeune sénégalaise dans des propos rapportés par WDRB , un média basé à Louisville. Amina Seck de poursuivre. « Seule dans cette pièce, sans personne d'autre, juste moi et moi-même, à regarder le mur, sans livres ni rien » Toujours d’après WDRB, Amina Seck aurait passé environ une semaine à l'isolement, après avoir refusé de retirer une attelle de genou dont elle avait besoin. Pendant sa détention, elle a subi une rupture du ligament croisé antérieur et une lésion du ménisque. Elle n'a pas pu passer l'opération qui était prévue. Son avocate, Sadiqa Reynolds, avait dénoncé l'absence de soins réguliers. Sa situation administrative n'est toutefois pas réglée. Le Département américain de la Sécurité intérieure affirme qu'un juge de l'immigration avait prononcé une expulsion définitive en septembre 2025, après son absence à une audience. Selon les autorités, elle était entrée légalement aux États-Unis en 2019, mais s'y était maintenue après l'expiration de son visa. Son dossier d'immigration reste ouvert. O.B.N

items.title: Israel drastically reduces British diplomatic presence in Jerusalem, announces closure of consulate
items.description: Israel said the British consulate in Jerusalem ended its functions on Thursday but that seven diplomats would be allowed to remain in a limited capacity, with the United Kingdom saying it would continue to offer “vital services”. The move comes after Israel ordered the closure of the consulate in September as retaliation after London led Western sanctions over violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Thursday’s move to downsize the UK presence had followed a dialogue with the British government in order to avoid an escalation of tensions between the two countries. “As I announced, the British consulate in Jerusalem ended its role today,” Saar said in a statement, adding that 20 diplomats including the consul general were ending their missions and leaving the country. Saar said the building is the property of the British government and that a “task force of only seven diplomats” would be allowed to operate from the premises, “which ceased to function as a consulate today”. “Their scope of activity will be very limited,” Saar said. Britain and Israel have “agreed on the continuation of dialogue between the governments, within which both sides will be able to raise issues important to them”, he said. The UK government pledged to continue delivering “vital services” in Jerusalem, saying the consulate general building would remain open and would “be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem”. “The UK Mission, Jerusalem is independent, operational and will continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people,” British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband said in a statement. Miliband said the UK did not accept that the Israeli government had “the legal right” to enforce the closure. “We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible,” he added. Israeli settlements An AFP photographer on Thursday saw that the diplomatic emblem and a plaque that adorned the consulate’s facade had been removed. The measure has led Britain to lose a “historic and meaningful presence” in terms of their support for the Palestinians and having a consulate general in Jerusalem, an Israeli diplomatic source said. “So yes, they keep the building” and a limited number of diplomats, the source told AFP , but “they have lost a historic and significant footprint”. The source said they thought the recent dialogue between the British and Israeli governments would allow a “turning point” in deteriorating relations. “If until a few weeks ago, until Sept 8, we were on a path of spiralling down, then I think the page has turned, and we are now on a path that will enable a return to more constructive, not only dialogue,” the source said. “Dialogue is a path towards returning to … more constructive relations,” they added. On Sept 8, Saar ordered the British consulate to close. He said Israel would also expel British representatives at a centre monitoring the US-brokered ceasefire plan in Gaza , bar British training for Palestinian Authority forces and ban 12 Britons, mostly members of parliament, from visiting. Saar on Thursday said the measures had been implemented. The retaliation came after 12 countries including Britain, Canada and France announced they would sanction trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, following a surge in settler attacks against Palestinians in the occupied territory. The British consulate in Jerusalem was founded nearly 200 years ago. It lies in east Jerusalem, part of the historically Palestinian area that Israel captured in 1967. Israel later annexed east Jerusalem and considers the holy city its undivided capital. While Israel controls east Jerusalem, most countries including Britain do not recognise its sovereignty over the whole city. The British consulate handles “political, commercial, security and economic interests between the UK and Palestine”, according to its website as well as providing consular services to British nationals in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza.

items.title: French teens march for decent schools despite government's pledge to act
items.description: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday as the government promised to address their grievances about teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings but gave few specific details. The protest movement, now into its third week, has exposed deep tensions in France between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and a cash-strapped government under pressure from bond markets to reduce its debt and deficit. High-school teacher Diane Di Sciullo joined students at a large march in Marseille, saying all they were asking for was a decent education in decent conditions. She denounced overcrowding, saying this year she had 37 students in her class. Protesters face French CRS riot police outside Lycee Helene-Boucher high school as students block the road, during nationwide protests in Paris, France, October 8, 2026, to demand better school conditions. —Reuters “At the start of every lesson, I have to ask them to check the neighbouring classrooms for spare chairs and desks so they can actually study,” she said. Di Sciullo, 28, was carrying a placard that read “I’m a teacher and my students help me catch cockroaches in class.” Protesters march during a demonstration by French high school students in Marseille, as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades, expressing anger over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings, which students blame on years of underinvestment, in Marseille, France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters Minister promises urgent action Education ministry figures showed the number of school blockades was gradually decreasing. It said 224 were closed in the morning, down to 157 by lunchtime, meaning that 96 per cent of schools were open. Scuffles between police and protesters took place at some blockade locations in Paris. Large crowds demonstrated across the country from Lille in the north to Rennes and Nantes in the west, the capital Paris, and Toulon and Marseille in the south. Police officers stand guard as French high school students block the road outside Lycee Helene-Boucher high school, as part of nationwide protests to demand better school conditions in Paris, France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters Education Minister Edouard Geffray held a meeting with students and teachers at a high school in the eastern city of Reims. “I am currently implementing an emergency plan to ensure that absent teachers can be replaced on a long-term basis,” he said afterwards, adding that heavy school timetables were also under review. It is not uncommon for French teenagers to have lessons from 8am to 6pm, as well as large amounts of homework. French high school and university students attend a demonstration in Nantes as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions in France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters Hundreds of arrests Geffray also said he was working on potential improvements to Parcoursup, the national online portal for applying to university, which has been widely criticised as confusing and stressful for applicants. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu pledged late on Wednesday that the government would present “concrete, quick and fully funded responses” to the protests by late October, without offering specifics. French students gather outside the Lycee Henri-IV in Paris as part of nationwide protests to demand better school conditions in France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters A prominent complaint featured on banners and placards was that the police response to the wave of protests has been too heavy-handed. “Too young to be listened to, old enough to be tear-gassed” was one example. There have been hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries since the movement started. On Wednesday, the government suspended the use of stun grenades in the policing of the protests after one teenager’s hand was blown off. Polarised political response as election looms Six months out from an election to replace President Emmanuel Macron after the end of his second consecutive term, politicians’ responses to the wave of student protests have been starkly polarised. Far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen has highlighted damage to schools caused by a minority of protesters and called for them or their parents to foot repair bills. On Tuesday, she outlined plans to slash public spending should she win. rotesters clash with French gendarmes, as French high school and university students attend a demonstration in Nantes as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades to demand better school conditions in France, October 8, 2026. —Reuters Her hard-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon, who also has a chance of making the runoff, has praised the protesters as “incredible” and denounced police brutality. According to an Elabe poll for BFM TV , 72pc of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate, but 55pc of them think the protests should stop. The government has sought to tread a line between condemning violent incidents in which schools were set ablaze and staff injured, while also expressing sympathy with some of the students’ complaints. Students protest in Belgium too On Thursday, student protests were also taking place in the Belgian cities of Brussels, Ciney and Liege. Grievances included rising costs, overcrowded classrooms, limited resources and increased teacher workloads. In Liege, where police said almost 200 arrests had been made in connection with student protests this month, authorities have imposed a ban on public gatherings of more than three people until October 16. However, police said a gathering in front of the city’s university had been authorised.

items.title: Hotel groups target Syria for tourism as it rebuilds from rubble of civil war
items.description: By Federico Maccioni and Siddarth S DUBAI, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Several global and regional hotel groups are looking to enter or expand in Syria, senior executives told Reuters, betting that its rich history and coastal destinations will attract overseas tourists as well as Syrians who have long lived abroad. items.title: Washington approuve plus de 2 milliards de dollars d’armes pour trois pays arabes
items.description: Les etats-Unis renforcent encore leurs liens militaires avec leurs partenaires du Moyen-Orient. Le departement d'etat a approuve plus de 2 milliards de dollars de ventes d'armes et de services militaires a l'egypte, au Koweït et aux emirats arabes unis, dans un contexte regional marque par la guerre contre l'Iran et par la multiplication des attaques de missiles et de drones, a rapporte un article de Middle East Eye paru le 7 octobre. Le Congres americain a ete informe de ces projets de ventes. Le contrat le plus important concerne les emirats arabes unis. Abou Dhabi souhaite acquerir jusqu'a 10 000 roquettes guidees APKWS-II, pour un montant estime a 1,04 milliard de dollars. Ces munitions, guidees par laser, peuvent etre employees contre des cibles terrestres mais egalement dans certaines missions aeriennes. Leur acquisition intervient alors que les monarchies du Golfe renforcent rapidement leurs capacites de defense face aux drones et missiles utilises dans les conflits regionaux. Garder l'ancienne architecture L'egypte devrait, pour sa part, acheter plus de 2 000 missiles antichars Javelin ainsi que jusqu'a 200 unites de lancement, accompagnes de pieces detachees, de materiels d'entraînement et d'un soutien technique. Le montant de l'operation est evalue a environ 832 millions de dollars. Cette annonce intervient quelques jours apres que Washington a leve des conditions liees aux droits humains sur 320 millions de dollars d'aide militaire destinee au Caire, invoquant les interets de securite nationale et le role strategique de l'egypte dans la region. Enfin, le Koweït consacrera environ 400 millions de dollars a la maintenance de ses systemes de defense aerienne Patriot et a l'achat de pieces detachees. Ces trois operations illustrent une meme priorite americaine : consolider l'architecture militaire de ses allies arabes a un moment ou l'equilibre regional est fragilise. Washington affirme que ces ventes ne modifieront pas fondamentalement le rapport de forces au Moyen-Orient, mais elles renforceront clairement l'interoperabilite entre les armees partenaires et les systemes americains.

items.title: Banks to suspend lending to public sector workers under Controller and Accountant General’s payroll
items.description: Banks have begun moves to suspend lending to public sector workers under the Controller and Accountant-General’s (CAGD) payroll scheme. This has become necessary due to the growing non-performing loans in the banking industry. The Chief Executive of the Ghana Association of Banks, John Awuah, told Journalists at the Association’s Annual General Meeting that the rising default of public sector loans has become a challenge, hence the action. He, therefore, believes that this will impact on the lending rate going forward. According to him, the action follows a marching order to the banks from the Bank of Ghana Governor, Dr. Johnson Asiamah, to reduce non-performing loans to less than 10.0% by next year. “We have begun discussions and in the coming weeks and days we are going to take an action to suspend total lending to public sector workers under the Controller and Accountant Generals payroll. This is serious because we cannot continue to do this to the industry [banking] where salaries are being paid but our loan repayments are not remitted”. “We shall be forced to do this to save the industry and I can assure you that this time, we shall go ahead”, he added. Furthermore, Mr. Awuah said “we have had all the discussions and whatever we need to say has been said but still we don’t get the results. This action was supposed to happen three months ago but few people from higher offices intervene and we had to pause. This time in the next few days or weeks, you’re going to hear from us”, he pointed out. The Association has also been charged to partner the Bank of Ghana in developing a framework for the full implementation of the Lenders and Borrowers Act.

items.title: Veteran communication scholar Idowu Sobowale dies at 85
items.description: LAGOS — Professor Idowu Akanbi Sobowale, a renowned communication scholar and veteran member of Nigeria’s media and communication community, has died at the age of 85. Sobowale died on Thursday morning, October 8, 2026, according to a statement by a member of his family, Akinniyi Sowunmi. Sowunmi announced the death in a statement titled, “Transition to Glory,” describing the deceased as a major loss to Nigeria’s communication community, particularly members of the Association of Communication Scholars and Professionals in Nigeria, ACSPN. The statement read in part: “This is a very sad day for us in the Communication Community in Nigeria and especially for us at the Association of Communication Scholars & Professionals in Nigeria. “Our father, Pa Deacon Professor Idowu Akanbi Sobowale, OON, 85, joined the saints triumphant this morning, October 8, 2026.” The family said details of the funeral arrangements would be announced later. Sobowale’s death comes as a loss to Nigeria’s communication and media community, where he was recognised as a veteran scholar and member of the professional community. The post Veteran communication scholar Idowu Sobowale dies at 85 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Lagos Life game is valued at $1bn — Creator, Shalom Rayhamen
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Nigerian software developer and creator of the viral Nigerian browser game Lagos Life, Shalom Rayhamen, has said the game is valued at $1 billion, dismissing a reported $100,000 offer for the game as too small. Rayhamen made the disclosure in an interview with Nigerian digital content creator Fisayo Fosudo, shared on his Youtube page on Wednesday. When asked what she thought about people online offering $100,000 to buy Lagos Life and whether she was willing to sell, Rayhamen said the amount was far below the value she places on the game. She said: “A $100,000 is small. Lagos Life is valued at $1 billion, so if they want to buy, they should talk $1 billion. What is a $100,000? I don’t want to say we’ve, like… or something, but what is that?” Lagos Life has become one of the most talked-about Nigerian-made digital games since its launch on October 1, 2026. The browser-based life simulation game allows players to create characters, take jobs, earn virtual naira, rent homes, socialise and explore locations inspired by Lagos. The game is essentially a Lagos-themed take on the life-simulation concept popularised by games such as The Sims, but its appeal comes from its use of familiar Nigerian experiences, locations and culture. Players can navigate different aspects of virtual Lagos, including employment, money, housing, entertainment and social activities. Among the locations featured in the game are Amala Shitta and Quilox, while its wider gameplay draws on familiar Lagos experiences such as transportation, nightlife and food. Lagos Life does not require users to download an application, as it can be played directly through a web browser on phones and computers. The game’s rapid growth has also attracted attention from businesses, with virtual advertising spaces providing a potential commercial model for the platform. However, the money used within the game has no real-world cash value. Players cannot withdraw the virtual naira or convert it into real money. Rayhamen’s $1 billion valuation comes as interest in the game continues to grow, following its rapid rise across social media and its large player base. The game’s success has also placed Nigerian-made browser games in the spotlight, following the viral attention received by Lagos Run, another locally themed game built around the experience of driving a danfo through Lagos. Vanguard News The post Lagos Life game is valued at $1bn — Creator, Shalom Rayhamen appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: I paid N6m for my son’s release, mother of freed NYSC member
items.description: A mother of one of the freed members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) says she paid N6 million ransom to secure her son’s release. Recall the prospective corps members were abducted on October 1 after gunmen attacked two 18-seater buses travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, along the Owerri-Onitsha expressway. The woman disclosed this in an interview with News Central Television on Wednesday, saying the kidnappers initially demanded N50 million for each victim before eventually accepting N6 million for her son. “Initially, they asked us to pay N50 million per head. We asked whether the amount was for all of them, but they insisted that no, it was for each person. Later, we started begging them to take N500,000. But they said no and started scaring us,” she said in Yoruba. “Three days ago, they called and said we should pay N15 million. We kept begging them that all we had was N5.5 million. They said no and insisted on N6 million. So, it’s that N6 million we paid.” The woman said the abductors asked the parents of the victims to send representatives to meet them in Ibadan as part of arrangements for the ransom payment. “They called all the parents of all the victims. Twenty of them are in the bush. They then asked us to send three persons each to meet with them in Ibadan. My husband and my son’s elder brother went. “When they got to the meeting place, they asked them to send the money to an account and that when they got to Imo state, they should change the money into dollars.” She said her elder son was among those who met the abductors and delivered the ransom. “It is not rumours. They have all been released and sent to us. His brother is among the people who went to meet with the abductors three days ago. They left with the ransom,” she said. “It was the brother who called us this evening to say that they had handed the ransom to the kidnappers and that they had released our son. We also spoke to the boy.” The mother, whose name was not disclosed, said the abduction left her traumatised and unable to sleep throughout the period her son was held captive. “Since he was kidnapped, I have been stooling. I couldn’t sleep either. But I was relieved when I heard they had been released. It was as though the chains all over me were loosened,” she said. The post I paid N6m for my son’s release, mother of freed NYSC member appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Usurpation d’identité: quand les escrocs se font passer pour des institutions
items.description: De plus en plus de démarches se font à distance: par téléphone, SMS, WhatsApp ou application. C'est pratique, mais les escrocs en profitent. Ils se font passer pour une banque, un opérateur téléphonique, les impôts, la sécurité sociale, la police ou un service de transport… Leur but: vous soutirer de l'argent à travers vos informations personnelles. Ces arnaqueurs utilisent plusieurs modes opératoires notamment le: – Vishing : ils vous appellent au téléphone ; – Smishing : ils vous envoient un SMS ou un message WhatsApp ; – Phishing : ils vous envoient un e-mail ou vous dirigent vers un faux site ; – Spoofing : ils copient un vrai numéro, une vraie adresse e-mail ou une vraie identité pour paraître crédibles. Les bons réflexes à adopter – Ne communiquez jamais vos codes de validation, mots de passe ou tout autre donnée personnelle à la suite d'un appel ou message, quelque soit l'interlocuteur. Aucune institution crédible ne vous les demandera. – Ne croyez en personne même si elle connaît votre nom ou détient des informations sur vous. – Si vous recevez de tels messages ou appels, raccrochez, puis contactez l'organisme sur les canaux officiels ou déplacez vous physiquement à leur siège; – Ne transférez pas d'argent et n'installez aucune application à la demande d'un inconnu ; – Vérifiez l'adresse du site avant d'y saisir vos informations ; – Partagez peu d'informations personnelles sur les réseaux sociaux ; – Consultez régulièrement vos comptes bancaires et Mobile Money pour repérer toute opération suspecte ; – Parlez-en à vos proches, surtout aux personnes âgées, qui sont souvent visées. Vous avez été victime Appelez tout de suite votre banque et votre opérateur pour protéger vos comptes et votre ligne. Gardez les preuves (captures d'écran, numéros, messages), puis déposez plainte. A retenir Une institution sérieuse ne vous demandera jamais, dans l'urgence, vos codes secrets ou un virement d'argent. Dans le doute: raccrochez, vérifiez, signalez Plateforme de lutte contre la cybercriminalité L’article Usurpation d’identité: quand les escrocs se font passer pour des institutions est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Pakistan Bar Council declares Ahsan Bhoon's law degrees genuine
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) on Thursday declared that the degrees of its elected members, including prominent lawyer Ahsan Bhoon, were genuine. The announcement by the PBC — the supreme regulatory body of lawyers — follows a debate over lawyers’ degrees, with the qualification of Bhoon, a member of the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP), particularly being questioned . In an official statement on Thursday, the PBC noted that the returning officers (ROs) for the council’s 2020 and 2025 elections had gotten the elected members’ degrees verified from their respective universities before notifying them as PBC members. “It is, therefore, clarified that the verification of the degrees of the returned candidates, including that of Bhoon, was undertaken through the relevant universities in accordance with the prescribed procedure,” the council said. It explained that the RO for PBC Election-2020 , the Attorney General for Pakistan (AGP), had the degrees verified by the universities soon after the elections, following which the successful candidates were notified as PBC members. Similarly, the RO for PBC Election-2025 , also the AGP, again initiated the process of verification of the elected members’ degrees. “Some members whose degrees were already verified in the last elections, their degrees too were sent again for verification to the relevant universities as well as the Higher Education Commission (HEC),” the council maintained. The statement comes over a week after former MNA and retired Capt Muhammad Safdar called for verification of the degrees of prominent lawyers, including Bhoon, a close associate of Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar. The debate also comes ahead of the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) elections scheduled for Oct 29. Bhoon, a former SCBA president, heads the Independent Group, also known as the Asma Jahangir Group. Safdar has announced the formation of his own group, the Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah Group. Days later, Safdar moved a complaint with the JCP to seek verification of Bhoon’s educational qualifications, enrolment and professional credentials. The complaint had also sought verification of his original degrees, transcripts, result cards and registration records; independent confirmation from the degree-awarding institution; verification from the HEC; his complete enrolment record with the relevant provincial bar council and the PBC; and the dates and basis of his enrolment as an advocate. On the other hand, Bhoon has served a Rs5 billion defamation notice on Capt Safdar, demanding an unconditional public apology and retraction of the allegation that his LLB degree was fake. According to the notice, Safdar made the allegations while speaking publicly outside the Supreme Court on or about Sept 23, with remarks repeated in later media appearances and video messages.

items.title: Umahi dismisses rift with Wike, says ‘we’re one family’
items.description: Minister of Works, Dave Umahi, has dismissed reports of a strained relationship between him and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, describing the former Rivers State governor as a progressive politician and member of the same political family. Umahi spoke at a press conference in Abuja on Wednesday while reacting to reports of divisions within the All Progressives Congress and speculation over his relationship with Wike. The minister said there was no basis for the reports of a rift, insisting that both men remained connected by their shared political interests. “We need Wike as Wike needs us. So, it’s one family,” Umahi said. He said political differences between him and the FCT minister had been exaggerated by their opponents, stressing that their relationship remained cordial. Umahi also urged politicians to focus on national development rather than allow political disagreements to create divisions among people who share common interests. Wike, who remains a member of the Peoples Democratic Party, has continued to maintain his political relevance while backing President Bola Tinubu’s administration. In January, the FCT minister said his rainbow coalition represented a departure from conventional party politics, describing it as a collective political movement aimed at advancing the interests of Rivers State. His position has, however, come amid concerns within the ruling APC over political alliances that could affect Tinubu’s re-election bid in 2027. The Progressive Governors Forum has said it would not support any alliance or political arrangement capable of undermining Tinubu’s re-election or the electoral prospects of APC candidates in the 2027 elections. Despite the concerns surrounding political alignments ahead of the 2027 elections, Umahi maintained that his relationship with Wike was not defined by the differences being portrayed by their political opponents. He reiterated that both men remained part of the same political family and should be viewed within the broader context of their shared commitment to national development. items.title: Viral video: FCT CP orders probe into N450,000 demand
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi ABUJA — The Commissioner of Police, FCT Command, CP Ahmed Muhammed Sanusi, has ordered an investigation into allegations that police investigators demanded N450,000 from a content creator before investigating a complaint he brought to the command. The allegation was contained in a video circulating on social media in which the content creator, identified as Tumma Gabriel, claimed that officers at the FCT Police Command Criminal Investigation Department demanded the money as “mobilisation and petition.” The command’s Police Public Relations Officer, SP Josephine Adeh, disclosed this in a statement on Thursday. Adeh said the FCT Police Command was aware of the video and stressed that the police did not mandate or encourage its officers to solicit or demand any form of payment before, during or after investigations. “The Command wishes to state clearly that it does not mandate or encourage its officers to solicit or demand any form of remuneration before, during, or after investigations,” she said. She said the Commissioner of Police had consequently ordered a thorough investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the allegation and identify any officer who might be involved. “Any person found liable will be dealt with in accordance with the provisions of the Police Act and Regulations,” Adeh added. The command also urged the complainant to contact it through 08180382808 and visit the Command Headquarters to assist the investigation by providing relevant information that could help identify the officer or officers involved. The police said the investigation was aimed at establishing the facts surrounding the allegation and taking appropriate action where wrongdoing was established. The post Viral video: FCT CP orders probe into N450,000 demand appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: GAUA strike leaves some KNUST administrative offices operating below capacity
items.description: The ongoing strike by the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) has begun to disrupt administrative services at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), with some students and national service personnel being asked to return at a later date to access services. Some offices, including those responsible for payroll and auditing, have been affected by the strike, while key student-facing units such as the Finance, Registry and Examinations offices remain open, albeit with reduced operational capacity. One of those affected by the disruption told JoyNews on Thursday, 8 October, that she had travelled to the university to have her National Service Scheme (NSS) documentation endorsed but was informed upon arrival that she would have to return later. The delay, he explained, could have financial implications for her because she had travelled to the university without making adequate preparations for a longer wait. She expressed hope that the industrial action would be resolved soon to enable affected personnel to return to work. “I hope that they call it off so that we can resume working.” KNUST GAUA chapter defends strike action The KNUST chapter of GAUA has defended the industrial action, stressing that the association’s members have a right to strike in pursuit of their demands. Speaking on the impact of the strike, the chapter’s General Secretary, Kwadwo Asenso Fanwel, said the association was mindful of the need to maintain its professional and ethical responsibilities even while participating in the industrial action. “We have clearly indicated that a strike is a right of every association or a grouping to press on their demand,” he said. Mr Asenso Fanwel, however, emphasised that GAUA members were not deliberately seeking to sabotage university operations. He explained that the disruption arising from the strike should be understood as passive rather than active. “The disruption here in this case will be passive. We are not going to cause any active disruption, but by virtue of the fact that our people are not going to be in the office to put back services, that is where the effect will be felt,” he explained. Strike intended to demonstrate importance of administrators Mr Asenso Fanwel also acknowledged that the effectiveness of industrial action depends partly on its ability to demonstrate the importance of the workers involved. He said GAUA believed the absence of administrators from their posts would highlight the essential role they play in keeping university systems and services running. For now, the KNUST situation demonstrates the wider role played by university administrators in ensuring that academic institutions function smoothly, even when their work is largely behind the scenes.

items.title: Popular Nigerian rapper Lord of Ajasa becomes US citizen
items.description: Veteran Nigerian rapper Olusegun Osaniyi, popularly known as Lord of Ajasa, has become a United States citizen, drawing congratulatory messages from fellow artistes, music producers and fans. The pioneer of mainstream Yoruba rap shared photographs and videos of himself celebrating the milestone on his Instagram page, @lordofajasa, on Wednesday. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Olusegun Osaniyi (@lordofajasa) In one of the clips, the rapper was seen holding his American citizenship certificate, while another photograph showed him posing with his wife alongside the United States flag. The development quickly attracted attention from fans and entertainment personalities, with several of Lord of Ajasa’s contemporaries celebrating the milestone in the comment section of his Instagram post. Music producer and Coded Tunes founder, Olumide Ogunade, popularly known as ID Cabasa, wrote, “Congratulations Lord Oshi.” Lord of Ajasa replied, “Thanks Cabasa.” His contemporary, singer Abolore Akande, popularly known as 9ice, also congratulated him, w riting, “Congrats apase” Lord of Ajasa responded, “Thanks Baalè.” The rapper’s citizenship milestone also renewed conversations about his contribution to the development of indigenous Nigerian hip-hop, particularly Yoruba-language rap. Lord of Ajasa emerged as one of the early artistes to bring Yoruba rap into mainstream Nigerian music, predating the rise of later indigenous rap acts such as Dagrin, Olamide and Reminisce. His music has remained influential in conversations about the early years of Yoruba hip-hop, with songs including “Le Fenu So,” “Esha Lo Bade,” and “Mai Lo” still remembered by music lovers. The veteran rapper’s latest milestone has now added a new chapter to his career, as fans and colleagues continue to celebrate his transition to American citizenship. items.title: Lecornu libère 10 millions de barils de gazole pour faire baisser les prix
items.description: Sebastien Lecornu a annonce, le 7 octobre au soir, la mobilisation d'une partie des stocks strategiques francais afin de tenter d'alleger la facture des automobilistes. Alors que le gazole avoisine 2,40 euros le litre, le gouvernement veut agir sur le coût d'approvisionnement des distributeurs plutot que recourir a une nouvelle baisse massive de la fiscalite. « Nous allons utiliser [ces reserves] de maniere nouvelle, pour agir sur les prix », a declare le Premier ministre depuis Matignon. Les 10 millions de barils, acquis avant la flambee des cours, seront mis a la disposition des distributeurs au prix de revient. Cette operation, etalee sur trois mois et effective des le debut du mois de novembre, doit « mecaniquement » faire baisser les tarifs de 12 a 18 centimes par litre. Les distributeurs seront reunis « dans les tout prochains jours » afin d'en preciser les modalites. Sébastien Lecornu : «Nous mettrons 10 millions de barils de gazole issus de nos stocks à la disposition des distributeurs en France» Toute l'info est à retrouver sur https://t.co/NVs1Rf6rXd https://t.co/0VTD5TVsJh — CNEWS (@CNEWS) October 7, 2026 Cette initiative s'inscrit dans le cadre d'une decision du G7 de liberer 100 millions de barils de produits petroliers . Elle intervient alors que les prix ont fortement progresse ces dernieres semaines, alimentes par les tensions geopolitiques. Sebastien Lecornu a en revanche ecarte une diminution massive des taxes sur les carburants. « Nous ne pouvons pas rouvrir les memes depenses a chaque crise […] surtout avec des taux d'interet plus eleves », a-t-il justifie, soulignant les difficultes budgetaires et l'objectif de limiter le deficit a 5 % du PIB. Marine Le Pen a reagi sur le ton de l'ironie : « Comme d'habitude, ils finissent par mettre en œuvre nos propositions apres les avoir ridiculisees. ». La baisse s'ajoutera aux aides deja en place pour les grands rouleurs, mais reste conditionnee a la cooperation des distributeurs et a l'evolution des cours mondiaux, dans un contexte d'incertitude de l'approvisionnement en France .

items.title: Messi’s farewell: Rohr reveals Benin players were denied photos, shirts
items.description: Benin head coach Gernot Rohr has criticised the treatment of his players after their international friendly against Argentina, saying they were denied the opportunity to take photographs with Lionel Messi and exchange shirts with the world champions. Argentina defeated Benin 3-0 at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires on Tuesday in Messi’s final appearance for the national team. Speaking on RMC radio’s Rothen s’enflamme on Wednesday, Rohr said the Benin players attempted to meet Messi and other Argentine players after the match but were prevented from doing so by security personnel. “Yes, it was extremely difficult. We tried. “The only shame is that the Argentines gave us nothing. No photo with Messi, no shirt. They didn’t even let us into the tunnel, nor even the dressing room,” he said. “Security refused to let anyone in. Some players came to swap shirts, so we knew it would be difficult. We tried everything, but we got nothing,” he added. The Benin delegation also tried to present Messi with a bouquet of flowers in the country’s national colours, but Rohr said the gesture did not lead to a meeting with the Argentine captain. “We offered a bouquet of flowers in Benin’s colours, yellow, red and green, but that didn’t work,” the German said. “However, I gave Messi’s 2018 shirt to coach Scaloni, who got him to sign it for me and then returned it to me, but that was all,” he said. Messi marked his farewell after a 21-year international career with Argentina with a goal and two assists, setting up Nicolás Otamendi and Nico Paz before converting a penalty as Argentina secured the victory. He ended his Argentina career as the country’s most capped player and leading goalscorer, with 208 appearances and 126 goals. The post Messi’s farewell: Rohr reveals Benin players were denied photos, shirts appeared first on Vanguard News .
